finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. Replacing the switch at the brake pedal is a small job on the vehicles examined: every maker-stated time found for one switch alone is 0.2 to 0.4 hour, and the longest time any acceptable source states is about half an hour. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2010 Elantra about $48-$80 (0.3-0.4 hr); midsize 2011 Sonata about $61-$115 (0.3-0.5 hr); truck 2006 Colorado about $58-$143 (0.2-0.5 hr); luxury 2008 Acura MDX about $102 at the low end and about $141 with list-price parts at the one stated time of 0.2 hour, because the upper labor time for that class is null. These built totals are lower than the three benchmarks ($80-$100, $82-$120 and a $183 average for one model): the economy total tops out at the bottom of the benchmark ranges. The likely reason is that every time used here is a warranty time, a maker's estimate to owners or a parts seller's install time, while a shop usually bills a minimum labor charge and often a diagnosis fee; no acceptable source stating that longer billed time was found, so it is not built in. How solid the labor times are: all four low ends are maker warranty times for the example vehicle and for one switch (Hyundai 0.3 M/H for the 2007-2010 Elantra and the 2011 Sonata, GM 0.2 labor hours for the 2004-2006 Colorado, Acura 0.2 hour for the 2007-11 MDX); the GM procedure also has the technician look at the switch retainer. The high ends now rest on three different sources, none for the example vehicle. Economy: Nissan's warranty time of 0.4 hr for the 2016-2019 Sentra, which covers the switch, a rubber grommet and taking the lower dash panel off and on. Midsize: Toyota's recall letter to 2009 Camry owners saying the switch replacement takes approximately 30 minutes, which is a maker's estimate, not a flat-rate time. Truck: a parts seller's stated install time of approximately 30 minutes for the Silverado 1500 and the Ram 1500, which are full-size pickups and not the Colorado, and is not a flat-rate time. Luxury: null. No bulletin, trade-press article or signed guide stating a time longer than Acura's 0.2 hour was found for a luxury vehicle. The earlier 0.8 to 1.2 hour figure from an unsigned general guide has been removed from every class. Longer maker times exist only for jobs that include more than the switch and are cross-checks only: Subaru 0.5 hours (kit with an adapter harness and a clevis pin), Honda 0.6 hour for the 2006 Civic (kit with a new connector that the wire terminals are moved into), Nissan 0.8 for the Maxima and 1.8 for the Frontier (jumper harness work; those two are not cited as sources for any range). Volkswagen prints 40 T.U. for its Jetta and New Beetle switch recall; that was not converted to hours because no conversion source was loaded. Because one labor end is null and three of the seven stated labor ends are not for the example vehicle, confidence is low. Parts: the high in every class is the maker's list price from a dealer parts catalog. No aftermarket switch was found on a page that states the part is new, so each low is a dealer-parts discounter's price for the genuine switch on a page that states it is new; aftermarket switches seen without a stated condition were $14.76-$15.49 for the Hyundais and $15.46 for the Colorado. Switch prices vary a lot within one model: the 2010 Elantra page also lists a $50.11 switch, and other Acura MDX years use switches that list from $12.40 to $125.46. This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or electrical testing fee, shop supplies and sales tax, and many shops bill a minimum labor charge. Bulbs, a blown fuse, a damaged connector or wiring repair are quoted separately. Some vehicles need the switch adjusted or a sensor relearned with a scan tool, and a few need a software update afterward. On some vehicles the pedal stopper pad that presses the switch is replaced at the same time.

The unsigned general guide is gone: the highs are now a Nissan 0.4 hr (Sentra), a Toyota owner-letter 30 minutes (Camry) and a parts seller's 30 minutes (Silverado, Ram), none for the example vehicle, and the luxury high is null. Held at review: every time is a warranty, owner-letter or seller time, so the built totals (about $48 to $143) sit below all three outside estimates ($80 to $183) and would call ordinary quotes high. Needs a stated time or minimum labor charge that reflects what shops bill.
